speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head L of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sustainability is at the heart of everything MSE does.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is code red for humanity and this race to zero is crucial.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Climate change is an existential threat that we cannot ignore and simply adapt to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A recent UN IPCC report warned that if countries do not do more to fight climate change, the climate will change faster than we can adapt to it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are especially heartened with this whole-of-Government and whole-of-society approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we will continue to work with businesses and citizens to co-create solutions to tackle climate change together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can share more about how we are increasing our climate ambition and action, how the revised carbon tax will support our inclusive green transition, how we will soften its impact on households and businesses, and how we are protecting our coastlines as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we chart the way forward, I hope we always remember that there is no Plan B because there is no Planet B.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond climate change, my GPC colleagues and I will be speaking on a broad range of issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We look forward to updates on the Green Plan 2030, our Zero Waste Masterplan, the disposable carrier bag charge, GreenGov.SG and the lifespan of the Semakau Landfill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We hope to strengthen our defences against public health threats, advance water and food resilience and security, make progress on our 30 by 30 plan and do more to support our hawkers, who have not had an easy two years during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And we will of course debate my pet topic of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure Senior Minister of State Amy Khor is looking forward to it and I promise her, no more stealth mode.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second-hand smoke is another threat that we cannot ignore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have been flooded with appeals for help, people fearing for their health and begging for fresh air.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hate to imagine what impact this has had on their health and the health of their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a race towards tackling this public health crisis, and like climate change, it is a race we should not and cannot lose.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are lots more questions and issues to raise and it is an incredibly diverse range of issues that we will be debating over the next six and a half hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The call is not to eliminate the use of disposable bags but to reduce it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Prime Minister Lee said: “It is a sensible approach: to make people conscious of the plastic bags they use, but not to ban plastic bags altogether.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand we want to start small but this problem is urgent and massive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can extend this charge to smaller convenience stores.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad Cheers has already done this and I saw firsthand how this works.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We usually make smaller purchases at convenience stores as compared to at supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means the disposable bag charge is a relatively larger amount and people feel the pinch more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When cashiers say, “Do you want a plastic bag?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is now chargeable”, I have seen so many people reply, “In that case, I don’t want it.” Purchases at convenience stores are also usually of a smaller quantity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many can simply hold or put the purchases in their own bags.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, many of the disposable bags used at convenience stores are smaller and can’t be used to line our rubbish bins.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Extending this charge beyond supermarkets can have a huge impact for this planet.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In 2018, in a Singapore Environment Council study, it found shoppers take 820 million disposable carrier bags from supermarkets a year, or an average of 146 bags per person.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If we look back at our past, we can understand why Singaporeans have such a voracious appetite for plastic bags.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many of us grew up with them from around the 1970s.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Admittedly, they come in very useful when you are at the wet market when buying fish, vegetables and many other uses.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many of us justify taking plastic bags from the supermarket because plastic bags can be reused for disposal of household rubbish.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Thus, these plastic bags become an omnipresent product, which can be found in the remotest of places from the seabed to the summit of Mount Everest.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Implementing a plastic bag charge will certainly reduce excessive plastic bags consumption but such implementation will also add to the increased cost of living, especially for lower socio-economic group.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister share details on the model of this impending bag charge?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How has the Ministry consulted stakeholders to develop the model for the disposable carrier bag charge?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How will this affect the cost of living, especially the lower socio-economic group?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What can be done to mitigate the cost for this group?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Apart from plastic bags, in fact, the current COVID-19 pandemic has brought about another set of problems with the use of plastics, that is, millions of discarded single-use plastic food containers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How are we dealing with the disposal of all these plastics in the current pandemic?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The announcement to implement a charge on disposable carrier bags at supermarkets as per the recommendations submitted by the Citizens Workgroup after consultation with the NEA and members of the public, is a move that is highly anticipated, and to some, viewed with some hesitation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Singapore, supermarket retailers such as NTUC Fairprice and Don Don Donki have already taken the initiative and begun to implement charges for their disposable bags.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While such measures look to disincentivise shoppers from using disposable plastic carrier bags offered in stores, there are some who have brought up that Singaporeans have always been recycling supermarket bags, using them as trash bags and such a model might create a situation where consumers take more bags than needed after paying the fee for them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is of these concerns that we would like to seek clarification concerning the proposed charging model when implementing the mandatory charge for carrier bags at supermarkets.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a smart nation of digital natives, we have become increasingly reliant on electronic devices to allow a society to function.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Incorporating more of such devices into our lives naturally means that we generate more of such e-waste, waste that contain hazardous materials and poses a health and environmental risk if not managed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the current e-waste collection and disposal scheme having been in place for half a year, we would like to seek clarification on whether the scheme has contributed to the increase in e-waste collection.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, we also seek assurance of the effects of the present scheme has on the ability to recycle the e-waste that we have generated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the Zero Waste Masterplan was introduced in 2019.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is an important blueprint for us to move forward towards being a sustainable city and it is essential we continuously move towards the targets we set for a greener Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government support the proper management of the three priority waste streams – namely food, e-waste, and packaging – to promote resource sustainability?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, what is the progress of the Zero Waste Masterplan and are we on track to reduce waste to landfills by 20% by 2026?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we encourage and support Singaporeans towards achieving our zero-waste target?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Its capital city, Ljubljana, attributed part of its success to strong communications strategies, campaigns and educational programmes to shift its citizens towards an eco-conscious culture.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They adopted a bottom-up approach, with communities’ involvement, cooperation from different stakeholders and implementation of nationwide programmes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Considering our aspirations towards reaching the zero-waste target and Singapore’s strength in whole-of-community approach, I will like to ask how MSE plans to enable families and communities to achieve our targets.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There is an overall decline in waste generation for the past four years, this is a good sign but is this sustainable when our domestic consumption has not significantly reduced, and recycling rates are not increasing proportionately within the industries and general public?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I wish to know what more are we doing to extend the lifespan of Semakau Landfill?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Here, I highlight two areas for improving waste management in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Discounting the effects of pandemic, the inherent problem lies with the long supply chains for food and losses during the handling and storage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To better manage the supply, we need more focus on technology applications and begin upstream in our food industry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For example, (a) to use technology like blockchains to assist the wholesalers, large importers and large users to provide key sourcing countries with more accurate information on supply demand patterns in variety and volume of food needs through the year.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This will help improve harvesting supply at right timing, production volume with less wastage and better understand the impact of increasing unseasonable weather; (b) to provide specific funding and more opportunities to connect the teams in ecosystem working on similar problem statements, for example, the food preservation with fresh producers using new techniques; and (c) conduct a comprehensive study to understand which part of the supply can be transformed locally or at source in order to mandate partially or in full the adoption of the Food Waste Minimisation Guidebook.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, on ferrous metal scraps, waste from construction and demolition, paper and card boxes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: All this waste will go into our landfill if not recycled or handled properly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Can NEA provide an update on the sustainable resource recovery solutions piloted thus far?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For high volume generated waste materials, what has the Government’s effort been in reducing them jointly with the industry?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I suggest a greater focus on waste reduction in immediate term, from more direct partnerships with business associations and corporations with large waste disposal to find ways to reduce and to reduce the packaging for local food delivery and introduce more environmentally friendly disposable packaging.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, with climate change, we can expect to experience more unpredictable and intense rainfall.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the years, we have been working on a number of projects to improve drainage and surface run-off and enhance storm water management.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Ministry share an update on these projects and future ones?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Maintenance and protection of drainage pathways are important, as we learnt from recent incidents where flash floods were caused by blockages and violations from engineering works in the vicinity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are PUB’s plans to mitigate inland floods?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the face of rising sea levels, we need to start on coastal protection.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Eventually, some of them will have to be built higher.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are the plans for these, including new seawalls, going forward?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And would the Ministry share updates on the progress of reclamation works as well?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The rest of our coastline are natural areas such as beaches and mangroves.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How does the Government ensure that coastal adaptation measures are cost-effective and adequately resourced; and how can the marine ecosystem be protected while these measures are being carried out?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Lastly, what progress has been made on coastal protection efforts since last year?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, last month I watched an interesting CNA documentary titled "Lost Waterfronts" which relate the history of Singapore’s former coastlines and waterfronts, which is now replaced by man-made landscapes such as Marine Parade, Changi Airport and MBS.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I was amazed by the tremendous transformation that our little island has undergone.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What was formerly our coastlines and beaches have all disappeared and replaced with land and development.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I wonder in 50 or 100 years from now, will our descendants be watching a different version of a similar documentary titled "The Lost Land", featuring the sea and describing what used to be a huge Changi airport and HDB Marine Parade estates is now replaced by sea.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: If we do not do anything to protect our low-lying areas against the rising sea level, that may become reality.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I still remember the graphic presentation during Prime Minister's National Day Rally in 2019, on Singapore's map showing all the low-lying areas which will be reclaimed by a rising sea level if nothing is done.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: And what Prime Minister said, that our descendants may ask: "why did we not do anything when we had a chance?" I, and many, are impressed by the ambitious plans shown during the presentation on building polders and a sea wall, not only to protect the low-lying areas but also to create new land and new possibilities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: And how does the Government ensure that the coastal adaptation measures are cost-effective and adequately resourced?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Chairman, during last year's Budget, as part of our climate adaptation measures, it was announced that Public Utilities Board (PUB) and JTC Corporation (JTC) will embark on site specific studies at the coastlines of City-East Coast and Jurong Island for coastal protection.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I understand that future studies for the northwest coast have also been planned.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I would also like to add to the questions raised by the previous Members before me, to ask how will the Government ensure that these measures are cost-effective?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: How will the Government plan to take into account existing ecosystems such as mangroves or intertidal zones as nature-based solutions, both in terms of conservation as well as potential solutions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unlike other countries, we do not have abundant high grounds.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With climate change, we can expect to experience more unpredictable and intense rainfall with sea levels rising faster.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What progress has been made on coastal protection efforts since last year and how can we protect our coastlines from rising sea levels, as well as erosion by waves and storms and reduce the land take for such measures to protect our coastlines?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How does the Government ensure that the coastal adaptation measures are cost-effective and well resourced?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because unlike local vehicles, NEA does not have the information on ownership of foreign registered vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This gives rise to an unhappy situation as NEA officers have to catch the offenders red-handed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This gap in enforcement policy must be closed, as NEA officers cannot be everywhere.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In May last year, I have filed a Parliamentary Question to MSC, subsequent to several cases of gastroenteritis in preschools, to enquire on what actions will be taken to manage such incidents and prevent them from recurring in future.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am delighted that Minister Grace Fu has in response, announced the intention to implement the Environmental Sanitation (ES) regime.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since then, I note that the ES regime has been implemented progressively to premises such as social service facilities, schools and preschools, as well as food centres, coffee shops and markets.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Ministry share the current progress on the regime's roll out and share more as to which other sectors or premises will it be expanded to, in order to prevent further gastroenteritis outbreaks from happening in the community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would places that offer food items to patrons, such as cinemas and spa facilities, be included as well?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken up a lot about protecting people from second-hand smoke in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is equally important to protect everyone in public areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad Orchard Road was designated as Singapore’s first No Smoking Zone (NSZ).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our surveys show that there is strong support for this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, I asked if the Government will designate other areas as NSZ.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has been a year, and I hope MSE has monitored this space closely and will roll out more NSZ and prohibit smoking in more places.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Despite knowing the harms of smoking and increasing prices of tobacco products in Singapore, the smoking rate in Singapore remains at about 10% in 2020.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: After the introduction of NSZ at Orchard Road, many are eagerly hoping that NSZ can be expanded especially nearing housing estates and provide permanent digital enforcement at the playgrounds, parks and common corridors of HDB blocks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Can the Ministry provide an update if there is any intent to expand NSZ in other areas of Singapore following the early pilots?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, the COVID-19 pandemic has rightly raised our concerns because of the toll it takes on innocent lives and the suffering of those who were inflicted with the disease.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Globally, since the outbreak of the pandemic, there were some 5.9 million deaths, and it is still rising.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There is another pandemic that is also claiming lives, but it is somewhat given a back seat.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The economic costs of tobacco use are substantial, for example, costs for treating the diseases caused by tobacco use as well as the loss of human capital that is a result from tobacco-attributed morbidity and mortality.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There are studies that shows that smoking is highly likely to worsen the severity of COVID-19 and the risk of dying from infection, according to a UK Biobank study published online in the respiratory journal of Thorax.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Despite all the health risks, cigarette smoking is one of the most common forms of tobacco use and it is one of the leading preventable risk factors for premature deaths, including non-smokers who are exposed to second-hand smoke.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We have been taking various steps to control cigarette smoking.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: But some countries, like New Zealand, are taking bolder steps to ban smoking.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Does the Ministry intend to roll out more NSZs and prohibit smoking in more places to protect the public from the harmful effects of second-hand tobacco smoke?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Do we have plans to introduce "end game" laws to snuff out cigarette smoking completely for our young Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is the results and lessons learnt from the 2014 Nee Soon South pilot project to ban smoking in public?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I urge the Government to take bold steps to extend more NSZs and finally also to consider smoking completely banned in all HDB estates.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The Chairman, the last extension of the smoking prohibition was in 2019, when Orchard Road was designated as Singapore’s first NSZ.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Does the Ministry intend to roll out more NSZs or prohibit smoking in more places to protect the public from the harmful effects of second-hand tobacco smoke, such as smoking corners at food retail establishments?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Many residents have been bothered by their neighbours’ second-hand smoke emitted from their windows and balconies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry please do more to curb second-hand smoke in residences, especially when complaints are from families with young children or residents with health problems and the neighbours are consistent and heavy smokers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, will the Ministry consider setting out a designated eco-friendly smoking zone at each HDB block for smokers to visit, instead of smoking at home and common corridors?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What other plans does the Ministry have to encourage residents who smoke at home to reduce the spread of their second-hand smoke in their homes and to surrounding units?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How effective has the wastewater testing surveillance strategy been for COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Ministry share if NEA intends to make this method of testing regular and routine in all areas for the long-term in order to monitor the spread of the pandemic?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Public toilets’ cleanliness and hygiene must meet NEA standards.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does NEA ensure that these standards are maintained?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the progress and improvement requirements for all toilets in hawker centres, markets and coffeeshops?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hawker centres provide a wide range of delicious and affordable food to our residents in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be new hawker centres in the next two years, especially in some of the newer estates?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, hawker centres are an important part of our heartland estates, providing a variety of affordable food to our multicultural population.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are also gathering points which serve to help with community bonding.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: COVID-19 has disrupted our everyday lives significantly, including slowing down the progress of work in our construction sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will we have enough hawkers to man the stalls at the new hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is no point having new and nice hawker centres with low utilisation rate.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How is the Ministry ensuring that we are training a pipeline of new hawkers to take over from the older cohort, many of whom will be retiring?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Chairman, as we transition to endemic living, our hawker scene has also undergone significant challenges.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Our hawkers are an important part of our heritage, and have seen some tough times during COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: However, some issues are evergreen, for example, urban bird management and ensuring clean hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I also hope that in due course, we will be able to reduce food, produce and packaging wastage in hawker centres, where everyone can play a part in food rescue efforts with the relevant overarching structures and support put in place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, can I take my two cuts together?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Like any other UNESCO cultural heritage, our hawker culture needs to be preserved and passed down for future generations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: However, it needs to transform with the times, in order to remain relevant for our people and for the livelihoods of our hawkers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: In the face of manpower shortage, especially in the hiring of hawker assistants and the shortage of young Singaporeans willing to pick up the hawker trade, I hope that we, as a nation, can consider this as a matter of urgency; we need to look into ways to support and transform this sector, which includes hawker centres, coffeeshops, canteens and food courts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: It has not been easy, but our hawkers have been trying very hard to keep their prices affordable.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Can we, therefore, help them reduce their costs with raw materials or improve productivity?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I have already seen some of our hawkers adopting machines to automate their cooking or other processes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We have seen how most of our hawkers have adopted digital payments and online ordering and delivery, through the support of efforts such as the Hawker Productivity Grant and the Alliance for Action.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Can more be done to bring down costs, such as by working with industry players to consolidate ingredient purchases by hawkers to achieve better economies of scale and lower prices for all?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We have to review all aspects of the nature of the industry and businesses, involve our hawkers in providing their feedback and inputs on how we can help them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I also hope that as we embark on the transformation and rejuvenation of our neighbourhood town centres, through initiatives by other agencies such as Enterprise Singapore’s Heartland Enterprise Centre, the relevant agencies can work together and take a holistic view, to ensure that our heartland enterprises and hawkers are all part of the overall rejuvenation efforts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: After all, our hawkers are heartland enterprises too.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I hope to hear more from the Ministry on its plans to transform the hawker trade.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: In a nation where many couples work full-time, many of our families depend on hawker centres to provide ready-cooked food.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Our hawkers are specialists in their niche areas, and this is how we can enjoy so many different versions of our favourite meals from across different ethnic cuisine groups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Singapore will not be the same without our hawkers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How can we improve the job prospects and working conditions, so as to attract more young hawkers?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Do we need restructure this occupation, so that they get covered for leave days, sick leave, medical care and insurance?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Presently, most hawkers work as independents and some do quite well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: However, for many, they really need to work many hours with very few rest days to earn a living, and falling sick becomes an extremely unthinkable costly problem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We must safeguard our hawker trade which is at the risk of vanishing when our older hawkers retire.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The work is tough and not many young people want to take over.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: However, our ageing hawkers want to pass their recipes and techniques for future generations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I would also like to reiterate my suggestion for NEA to facilitate the transition and help the veteran hawkers be paid an appropriate compensation amount, while the skills are being taught to the apprentice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The compensation sum should reflect the value of the heritage recipe and technique.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: In turn, the apprentice would have to serve out the bond at the stall for a period of, say, three years, for example.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I hope this will help to safeguard our hawker trade.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Our hawker trade is a key part of Singapore's history and identity.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We have strong public support for hawker culture, and many of us celebrated when our Hawker Culture was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in December 2020.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, plant-based meat is increasingly taking its place on our supermarket shelves, and I generally believe there is a gradual acceptance of this alternative meat substitute for real animal meat.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We are reliant on many countries to supply many essential items including meat.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: And if we are able to develop such alternative meat products locally, this would address some of our concerns in this area.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Besides, meat substitutes which are produced in laboratory by cell culture would contribute to our efforts to address climate change issue as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Thus, to meet the nutritional needs of a growing population and, at the same time, protect earth's fauna and flora, and fight against climate change, we need to consider and promote food products like meat substitute that are manufactured using plant-based products and meat produced in the laboratory by cell culture, instead of from animals in farms.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: This can form part of our 30 by 30 plan.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is Singapore's role in this new emerging sector?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How can we promote and grow this sector to benefit from this sector?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Safeguarding our food security is among the most important priorities for Singapore in our sustainability journey.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Government plan to help the local food production industry build up capabilities and capacity to achieve our 30 by 30 goal and enhance the resilience of Singapore's food supply?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As we achieve success in increasing our local food production, is the Government looking to calibrate food imports to avoid wastage?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Unlocking Singapore's sea space for sustainable aquaculture can help boost our local food production in the long term.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: However, as with our land resource, there will be diverse and competing needs for the use of our sea space.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Government plan to provide the local food production industry with greater certainty on the use of both land and sea space to optimise the supply of local produce?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Chairman, may I take my two cuts together, please?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I am heartened that much progress has been made in the last year towards the 30 by 30 plan, to reduce our reliance on food imports.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: However, concerns of space and sustainability, including that of sea spaces, are always a concern.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: What are the Government’s plans to optimise sea spaces for food production?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: And given the heavy investment required, does the Government have plans to provide the industry with greater certainty on the use of land or sea space?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Will measures be put in place to ensure a more sustainable aquaculture industry?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Last year, it was announced that the Government is working on a framework to shore up defences against marine litter to protect our coastline and surrounding waters.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Some of my youth volunteers and I had the opportunity to join environmental activists, students and clean-up crews at a Kayak and Clean event, where we found discarded nets, plastics and other types of marine litter floating around our island.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I have also had the opportunity to do dive clean-ups off our Southern Islands with marine scientists and volunteers from Our Singapore Reefs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: From youths to seniors, expats to Singaporeans, I am grateful for active and caring citizens who run efforts such as the East Coast Beach Plan, Green Nudge, One Planet and even our own Young PAP who have played a part in keeping our shores clean.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Can the Ministry consider a citizen committee, for example?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Food security is an existential issue for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The global food system faces many challenges, from short-term disruptions, such as disease outbreaks in a source country and the pandemic, to long-term issues such as climate change, global population growth and dwindling resources.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: It is important for the Government to work towards the 30 by 30 goal in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Further to this, unlocking sea space for sustainable fish farming can help boost our local production in the long term.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: However, as with land, there will be diverse and competing needs for the use of our sea space.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Chairman, the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and the global supply chain crisis highlight how important it is for Singapore to become more self-sufficient for our food supply.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: I am glad that the Government is embarking on a holistic exercise to master plan the Lim Chu Kang area into a high-tech agri-food zone.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: This bodes well for our future food security.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Is the Ministry involving them and inviting them to participate in the new plan?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: They should be given assistance, to start off, and incentives to upgrade their operations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: What other plans does the Government have to help our agri-food industry build up capabilities and capacity to achieve the 30 by 30 goal?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Mr Chairman, we have water supply from the Four National Taps: water from local catchment, imported water, NEWater and desalinated water.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: While desalination and NEWater are weather resilient and free from the vagaries tied to imported water, they are energy intensive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: In view of the current global energy challenges and Singapore’s commitment to transit to greener energy sources, how will PUB leverage on R&D and technology to enhance water efficiency and treatment?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: And what is the progress of our research projects in this field and are we collaborating with any foreign partners on this endeavour?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, may I have your permission to take two cuts?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Desalination and NEWater are two of our four sources of water supply, in addition to imported water and water catchment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The challenge with these two sources is that they require a lot of energy to process and treat the water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How would PUB improve on the energy efficiency of our water treatment to ensure its sustainability?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: PUB launched the Active, Beautiful, Clean Waters (ABC Waters) Programme to harness the full potential of our waterbodies – a network of 8,000 kilometres of waterways and 17 reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry share if there will be any new ABC projects in the next two years?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I applaud the efforts of the Ministry in undertaking long-term infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Joint efforts that use science, technology and our strong engineering capabilities to deliver highly accretive outcomes for sustainability mission.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In addition, much effort was also taken to use an ecosystem approach to leverage on the strengths of each project to further enhance outcomes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The Tuas Water Reclamation Plant, an integrated waste management facility are prime examples.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It was mentioned that the Tuas Nexus will tap on the synergies between water, waste treatment and energy – to use water sludge from Tuas when co-digested with food waste will improve bio-gas generation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I support these efforts by SME and the beyond horizon thinking and bold execution of these officers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To follow up, can I ask the Ministry on the progress of the Tuas Nexus and Tuas Water Reclamation Plant.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I start by congratulating the PUB for being successful in closing the "water loop" through integrated water management, by collecting as much water as we can and reusing water where possible.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: PUB had previously announced that the Deep Tunnel Sewerage System Phase Two is to be extended by 2025 to serve the western part of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is an important project that will go towards safeguarding Singapore’s strategic interest in water.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: From water conservation to building our own water taps.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Since the pandemic started, our hygiene alertness has significantly heightened.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: There is more extensive washing and higher frequency of cleaning in households, public areas and workplaces.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: While we hope these good hygiene habits continue to prevent the next potential spread of disease, I would like to ask whether the Ministry observed more water usage for maintaining such hygiene standards?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Does the work-from-home setting change the consumption usage by the households and what are the other initiatives the Government plan to introduce to improve water conservation?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: While raising awareness and changing consumption habits are important, we need to complement efforts beyond these.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: As Singapore is currently unable to harness all of the rainfall for usage, I would like to know how PUB is planning to maximise capacity of the underground water storage systems?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: At the same time, are more energy efficient technologies being explored for water treatment?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: With hybrid work arrangements expected to continue as COVID-19 becomes endemic, what are some of the initiatives that PUB or the Government will be taking to encourage more water conservation among households?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their questions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And thereafter we will have Members deliver their cuts on the joint segment on the Singapore Green Plan 2030 which will be addressed by Senior Minister Teo and several Green Plan Ministries, including clarifications that may arise.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These are among the biggest threats confronting the world today.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The pandemic has laid bare the fragilities of global supply chains, the vulnerabilities of healthcare systems and the cost of being underprepared.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The effects of climate change could be far worse.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Climate change will adversely impact economies and livelihoods, as well as security of essential resources such as water, food and energy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: COVID-19 has taught us the importance of resilience and this has relevance in the way we deal with climate change.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Whether a disruption is brought about by extreme weather events, or a global pandemic, we must take action today to assess our risk exposure, prepare our people and put in measures that will enable us to bounce back from disruption.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In this COS, Senior Minister of State Amy Koh, Minister of State Desmond and I will share how MSE is strengthening our resilience across three areas: resource resilience; climate resilience; and public health resilience.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As a globally connected economy with no natural resources, we are vulnerable to external shocks and supply disruptions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This has been made abundantly clear by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As our demand for resources continues to grow, so will our exposure to such fluctuations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Excessive consumption of resources also generates waste and emissions, worsening the climate crisis.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must reduce waste and maximise resource efficiency.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We also need to diversify our supply sources and promote circularity to reuse and recycle resources.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is no mean feat, but we have shown that it can be done.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have closed the water loop by reclaiming used water to become NEWater, allowing us to reuse every drop of water endlessly.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister of State Desmond will share how we are strengthening the resilience of our food and water supply.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Nadia Samdin and Miss Cheryl Chan have asked for an update on our waste reduction efforts.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In an increasingly resource-constrained world, we need to shift to a circular economy, where trash is turned into treasure and reused endlessly.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As we strive to become a Zero Waste Nation, we need to: encourage sustainable production, build capabilities to maximise resource recovery and collectively adopt sustainability as a way of life.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One key upstream measure to encourage sustainable production is the Extended Producer Responsibility, or EPR scheme.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: EPR requires producers, such as manufacturers and importers, to be responsible for the collection and proper treatment of their products at end-of-life.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We implemented the e-waste EPR last year to ensure the proper handling and treatment of e-waste.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This reduces our waste to landfill and allows us to recover valuable resources like gold and copper from e-waste, for use in manufacturing new products.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked for a progress update.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This accounts for approximately 8.5% of the consumer electronic and electrical equipment supplied in 2020.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The e-waste collected includes large home appliances like refrigerators and air-conditioners, and ICT equipment like mobile phones and laptops.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members of the public can drop off e-waste at more than 500 e-waste recycling bins nationwide, at convenient locations such as community centres, supermarkets and electronics stores.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: ALBA also works with Town Councils to organise quarterly collection drives at housing estates and collection of bulky e-waste.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For a fee, members of the public may contact ALBA to arrange for doorstep collection of e-waste.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Efforts are also ongoing to develop an EPR for packaging waste, starting with a return scheme for beverage containers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Under such a scheme, a deposit is included in the price of the pre-packaged beverages.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Consumers will receive a refund upon returning the used beverage container.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To facilitate development of this scheme, NEA formed a stakeholder group comprising key industry, academia and civil society representatives in December last year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Over the past two years, NEA has engaged more than 100 large and small producers, which make up about 80% of the pre-packaged beverage market.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This included industry briefings, surveys and one-on-one engagements with individual companies and trade associations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Other stakeholders consulted included retailers, waste management companies and members of the public.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA will continue to broaden engagement with the public and industry in the coming months, to co-design a cost-effective and suitable Beverage Container Return Scheme for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As we strive towards a Zero Waste Nation, we need to continue to ensure the sustainability of essential waste disposal services, while encouraging waste reduction to conserve Semakau Landfill.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Over the years, the operational costs of waste disposal have increased.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This fee is paid by general waste collectors and toxic industrial waste collectors to dispose of non-incinerable waste at Semakau Landfill, such as treated toxic industrial waste and sludge.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA will issue notification letters to the industry to allow the industry sufficient lead time to adjust.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We encourage all businesses to adopt sustainable practices to generate less waste and recycle more and play their part in the shift towards a greener and zero-waste Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As we put in place a comprehensive regulatory framework to encourage recycling, we also need to build capabilities in our local industry.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: A thriving local recycling industry can generate economic value, job opportunities and exportable solutions for the global green demand.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: EWR2 is a local e-waste recycling company that recycles large household appliances and ICT equipment and was set up in response to the increasing demand for e-waste recycling services driven by the EPR scheme.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It operates a highly automated recycling facility that can recover up to 95% of materials used to make the appliances, of which about 80% is being recycled.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are also pursuing chemical recycling of plastics that converts plastic waste into pyrolysis oil, which can be used as feedstock for the manufacturing of chemicals and plastics.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA commissioned a feasibility study on the development of a plastic recovery facility last year to extract plastics from our waste for chemical recycling.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The facility will harness advanced plastic waste sorting capabilities and improve our plastic recycling rates.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are finding other new innovative ways to turn waste into resource.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Semakau Landfill, for example, can potentially be mined for its landfilled materials.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA and the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore are carrying out a feasibility study to use such materials in its reclamation for Tuas Port.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If feasible, this will prolong the lifespan of Semakau and at the same time, reduce the amount of reclamation materials to be imported.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our transition to a Zero Waste Nation will require everyone to play their part.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To be a nation known for sustainable development, care for the environment must be reflected through our daily practices.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our personal and societal values drive the actions and choices we make daily.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The use of disposables is an issue that many Singaporeans care about.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While disposables have become an everyday convenience, they create large amounts of waste and use up finite resources.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We convened a Citizens' Workgroup in September 2020 to co-create solutions with the public in the spirit of Singapore Together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The workgroup came up with recommendations on how we can reduce the use of disposables such as carrier bags, food containers, cutlery and packaging.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Implementing a charge for disposable carrier bags at supermarkets was one of the recommendations of the workgroup.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our earlier considerations for not implementing a disposable carrier bag charge in Singapore are still valid.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Plastic bags are used by many households to bag our garbage before throwing it down our rubbish chutes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Unlike many other countries, we do not directly landfill our disposables but incinerate them.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Hence, we do not face the land and water pollution issues that plague those countries.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Climate action and environmental protection are gaining pace internationally and locally and we cannot continue with business as usual.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: A bag charge is becoming commonplace in jurisdictions around the world and closer to home such as in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There is broad recognition that we can reduce wastage of plastic bags.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In Singapore, an increasing number of retailers have voluntarily implemented a charge on disposable carrier bags, which has shown to be effective in encouraging the use of reusables.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: More importantly, we want Singaporeans to be a part of the shift towards a green Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We should show our care for the environment in the choices we make every day.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: By making the cost of the bag visible to consumers, the intent of the bag charge is to nudge people to consider what they really need instead of taking bags freely.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It will not remove the public's access to disposable bags.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is a nudge to every one of us to develop the habit of bringing a reusable bag when shopping for groceries and more and to reduce the use of disposables, an essential feature of sustainable living.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked about our consultations in developing the bag charge framework.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have conducted extensive consultations over the past year, including with supermarkets and members of the public.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have heard diverse views in our consultations and have considered these views carefully.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will be applicable to all disposable carrier bags.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have kept the minimum charge low to moderate the cost impact on shoppers, including on low-income households.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The more bags we take, the higher the amount we pay.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are starting with the larger supermarket operators who have extensive market coverage.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will not extend the charge to smaller convenience stores for now, as suggested by Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: During our consultation, concerns have been expressed about supermarket operators potentially profiteering from the charge.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We strongly encourage supermarket operators to channel the proceeds obtained from the bag charge to environmental or social causes and consider initiatives to support lower-income families.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The public will then be able to see how the supermarket operators are using their proceeds.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Over time, we hope that the charge will encourage Singaporeans to adopt sustainable habits and bring our own bags when shopping at supermarkets and other stores.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At this point, I would like to quote Ms Liu Yining who eloquently expressed on the need to reduce the use of plastic disposables in a recent commentary in Lianhe Zaobao.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: (In Mandarin):   On 4 March, Ms Liu Yining wrote a commentary in Lianhe Zaobao titled "Charging for disposable carrier bags sows a seed for de-plasticisation", She wrote that "the moment people take an extra plastic bag, they will have to think about whether they really need it or not, and at that point in time, a seed of happiness and kindness is sowed in the heart, and it is a seed of hope for themselves, the country and the world." (In English): The larger purpose of the bag charge is to make all of us pause and think if we really need the next bag before we reach for the bag.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is a seed of hope for a better world – the first step on a journey towards sustainability and the beginning of a change in how we treat the environment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling asked how we can encourage and support families and communities to recycle more.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Applying an idea from the Recycle Right Citizens' Workgroup to encourage right recycling behaviour, we recently piloted the use of transparent recycling bins in Hong Kah North and East Coast Group Representation Constituency (GRC).

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To encourage recycling at every home, NEA is collaborating with the Singapore Institute of Technology to design a compact recycling container to better sort out and collect recyclables at home.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These containers will be made available to households later this year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To minimise wastage, NEA will only distribute to households that want them.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our individual actions will determine the collective outcome of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Together, our zero-waste efforts will bring us closer to achieving our waste-to-landfill targets and extend the lifespan of Semakau for as long as possible beyond 2035.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Poh Li San, Ms Nadia Samdin, Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Sharael Taha asked about our progress in shoring up our coastal and flood defences.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Sea level rise poses an existential threat for a low-lying island nation like Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If there should be a confluence of extreme high tides and storm surges, some projections suggest that sea levels could be as high as four to five metres.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is high enough to potentially flood one third of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Coastal protection is a long-term endeavour and we have started planning ahead.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In May last year, PUB, the national coastal protection agency, embarked on a site-specific study at the coastline of City-East Coast.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singapore has a varied coastline of over 300 kilometres.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Hence, our site-specific studies allow us to understand the characteristics of these different segments and develop coastal protection solutions accordingly.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, there are four coastal reservoirs – Tengeh, Poyan, Murai and Sarimbun.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will study how to reinforce the dykes and dams for these important water sources to protect them from seawater intrusion.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Next, we will study how best to dovetail coastal protection solutions with upcoming developments such as the future Sungei Kadut Eco-District and Lim Chu Kang high-tech agri-food cluster.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There are also sections of mangrove habitats at the Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve and the Mandai Mangrove and Mudflat Nature Park.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must take care to minimise environmental impact in these biodiversity-rich areas.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: PUB will explore hybrid coastal protection solutions that combine nature-based elements with hard engineering measures and will also work closely with NParks and stakeholders to conduct environmental studies, minimise impact and enhance existing ecosystems.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These studies are expected to take a few years.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Even as we plan long term for the challenges of sea level rise, we are already seeing more extreme weather patterns today.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We see more flash floods from more intense rains.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Poh Li San and Ms Nadia Samdin asked what PUB's plans are to mitigate inland floods.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While we systematically improve our drainage system across the island, it is not possible to expand our drains to cater to every extreme rainfall event as it will mean less space for housing, parks or roads in land-scarce Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Hence, it is important to strengthen community resilience and our collective response to flooding incidents.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: PUB has been enhancing its early warning systems to provide more timely updates to the public, including launching a dedicated Telegram channel last November.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This allows PUB to provide timely assistance during any heavy rain event.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We urge Singaporeans to be on alert for weather events, by subscribing to PUB’s flood alerts for timely updates on heavy rains and potential flood risk locations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Building owners must do their part in protecting their properties by installing effective flood protection measures.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In July last year, PUB trialled the automated flood barrier at the entrance of Fortune Park Condominium leading to the basement carpark.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The automated barrier uses approaching floodwaters to buoy itself up and block floodwaters from entering the premises, without the need for any human or mechanical intervention.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is a viable and cost-effective solution for flood protection, and we encourage building owners in low-lying areas to implement these automated barriers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Chairman, as a small island city-state with no natural resources, we have weathered many crises together as a people and as a nation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have overcome these crises and seized the opportunities to develop into a clean, green and liveable city that we see today.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Climate change is the defining crisis of our generation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Together, let us build a resilient Singapore, for a sustainable future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: COVID-19 has reinforced the importance of good personal hygiene and clean public spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These have always been our priorities and will better prepare us beyond COVID-19 for Disease X, which is not a matter of “if” but “when”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Over the past two years, we have improved the cleanliness of public spaces – from working with premises managers to uphold high cleanliness standards, to ensuring individuals practise personal responsibility by returning trays and binning litter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have also achieved a national average TCRR of above 85% in coffeeshops and food courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Many have shared that the dining environment is now cleaner, with faster turnover of tables and fewer incidences of pests and bird nuisance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will build on this progress to ensure a clean and safe Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We commenced the progressive roll-out of the Environmental Sanitation (ES) Regime last July, which specifies mandatory baseline ES standards for high-risk premises and places greater accountability on premises managers to meet these standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We introduced the ES regime in more than 3,000 premises under the inaugural phase, including preschools, MOE schools, food centres, markets and coffee shops, and the first tranche of eldercare, youth and social service facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Together with the sector leads, we developed sector-specific ES standards and trained more than 3,600 Environmental Control Coordinators (ECCs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The ECCs will assist premises managers to develop and oversee the implementation of an ES programme, which specifies cleaning frequencies and disinfection protocols.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To Ms Hany Soh’s query, the regime was rolled out to preschools in November 2021 and all have appointed personnel to be ECCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The ES regime ensures that premises are properly cleaned and disinfected regularly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, from March this year, coffeeshops are required to carry out thorough cleaning every quarter on top of routine cleaning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is a marked difference from just ad hoc cleaning before.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: High-touch surfaces would also be cleaned and disinfected more frequently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Premises managers are also sensitised to their responsibility to prevent outbreaks of infectious diseases like gastroenteritis within their premises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, preschools have found the regime useful in providing clear guidance on minimum cleaning and disinfection frequencies, and scope of cleaning and disinfection works, neither of which were clearly defined before.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These would include publicly accessible premises with high footfall such as large shopping malls, as well as private education institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have worked with these sectors to develop sector-specific ES standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Another important aspect of a clean and safe environment is protecting Singaporeans against the harmful effects of second-hand tobacco smoke.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Today, smoking is prohibited in more than 49,000 premises, including covered walkways and common areas of residential buildings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have prioritised places where second-hand tobacco smoke affects more people, such as community spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition to neighbourhood parks in public and private housing estates where smoking is already prohibited, smoking will be prohibited at Regional and City Parks like East Coast Park and Fort Canning Park, and all Park Connectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Smoking will also be prohibited at 10 recreational beaches, including three beaches in Sentosa.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We currently have no plans to set up additional No Smoking Zones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will review the need for further extensions of the smoking prohibition from time to time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Setting up No Smoking Zones requires significant stakeholder buy-in and operational resources to implement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will need to plan extensively, assess the suitability of the precinct and availability of sites for designated smoking areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: On smoking in homes, which Dr Lim Wee Kiak, Ms Poh Li San and Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about, legislation is no panacea to curbing second-hand tobacco smoke in homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: There are privacy concerns and technological limitations to gathering evidence required for enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Designated Smoking Points (DSPs) in Nee Soon South have thus far not resulted in a sustained reduction in feedback received on smoking in homes in the division since its implementation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Nevertheless, we will continue to monitor the effectiveness of DSPs as localised solutions, even as we work with MOH and HPB to discourage smoking at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides adopting preventive measures to minimise the spread of infectious diseases, we are building up capabilities to deal with public health threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Singapore is an early adopter of wastewater surveillance for COVID-19, which is being explored in various countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In response to Mr Gan Thiam Poh's question, when transmission first occurred at workers’ dormitories, NEA brought in wastewater testing to assess the situation, including the viral loads collected from each dormitory.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our findings were used to complement individual testing, guide infection control measures and facilitate the progressive clearance of dormitories by the Inter-Agency Task Force.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Monitoring has since been expanded to student hostels, nursing homes, and residential sites.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: From a modest eight sites in May 2020, we gradually expanded surveillance coverage to 200 sites in July 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As Singapore transits to COVID-19-endemicity, the focus of wastewater testing has shifted from early case detection to providing situational awareness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The data collected alerts Government agencies and premises owners or operators of the situation, which allows them to calibrate public health measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It provides objective information on whether infections among the population are increasing or decreasing, independent of the population’s health-seeking behaviour and prevailing clinical test protocols.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will therefore be an important surveillance tool even as we transit to an endemic state.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Further research and development will allow the wastewater surveillance system to be used for monitoring other infectious disease threats in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about improvements to toilets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We launched the Toilet Improvement Programme in October 2020 to raise the cleanliness of toilets in hawker centres and coffeeshops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The programme supported premises in improving toilet design and choice of sanitary fittings for easier cleaning and coffeeshop operators' initial adoption of fortnightly deep cleaning on top of daily cleaning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA has received applications from 62 eligible coffeeshops and 28 hawker centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Twenty-four coffeeshops and one hawker centre have completed their toilet enhancement works.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I will now speak about our hawker culture, my favourite topic!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our hawkers are frontline heroes, providing us affordable hawker food during this pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA has provided relief measures to hawkers over the last two years, including 10 months’ rental waivers and six months’ subsidies for table-cleaning and centralised dishwashing services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Eligible hawkers also received up to $9,000 via the Self-employed Person Income Relief Scheme (SIRS) in 2020 and a one-off cash payout of $500 under the Market and Hawker Centre Relief Fund (MHCRF) last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Minister for Finance announced that small F&B businesses, one of the sectors most affected by COVID-19, will receive the Small Business Recovery Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Those without local employees will receive a flat $1,000 if they are Singapore Citizens or Permanent Residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our efforts have helped hawkers during these tough times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: On average, 17 cooked food stallholders or 0.3% terminated their leases each month between 2020 and 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is lower than the monthly average of 28 terminations between 2017 to 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked if more can be done to help hawkers reduce ingredient cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will review her suggestion of bulk purchasing carefully and also consider the interest from our hawkers, where many may already have established relationships and specific arrangements with their suppliers for their preferred ingredients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To prepare hawkers for the digital economy and expand their reach to potential patrons, hawkers, community groups, food delivery platforms, together with NEA and IMDA came together to form the SGTogether Alliance for Action (AfA) for Online Ordering for Hawkers last June and developed pilot initiatives to help hawkers utilise online services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: About one in every four cooked food stallholders have been supported via NEA’s Food Delivery Support Scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: WhyQ, Deliveroo, FoodPanda and Grab have stepped up to pilot a Common Acquirer Model for online food delivery in 15 hawker centres at zero commission to hawkers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Hawkers can receive online orders from any of these platforms through a single ordering device.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Alternatively, they can choose to transact offline through WhyQ hawker captains.
