speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To date, 18 hawker centres have set up Digital Support for Hawkers groups, which provide peer support to help less digitally savvy hawkers embrace digital opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This includes creating Facebook pages for each centre, facilitating online community group buys, and organising bulk meal orders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I am pleased to share that many of my fellow Members of Parliament have adopted AfA’s recommendations on group buys from hawkers for our lunches during Parliament sittings!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For today’s lunch, many of us enjoyed wanton noodles, chicken rice and burgers from Commonwealth Crescent, Bukit Merah and Golden Mile!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: More enticing and mouth-watering hawker dishes to come!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Nadia asked for an update on the Hawker Centres Transformation Programme (HTP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Last year, I shared plans about the HTP to future-proof hawker centre infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The proposed scope of works may include High-Volume Low-Speed fans to improve ventilation, provisions to support flexible implementation of Safe Management Measures, such as quick deployment and removal of temporary access control, reconfiguration of tables and chairs to reduce crowding, and additional handwashing facilities to raise hygiene levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA has also been receiving enquiries from individuals who are keen to take up stalls at the new centres, and the monthly tender for vacant stalls at existing centres have continued to attract a good number of bids.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Pereira asked about efforts to attract new hawkers, including improving job prospects and working conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our hawkers today are mostly self-employed individuals, with the flexibility and autonomy to decide their operating hours based on what they sell.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They are covered by Medishield Life and can also top up their medical insurance individually, or even explore purchasing together as a group through their Hawkers’ Associations (HAs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have been helping our aspiring hawkers prepare for the trade, through the Incubation Stall Programme and Hawkers’ Development Programme, and similar programmes by Socially-conscious Enterprise Hawker Centre operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Their median age is 33, significantly lower than the overall median age of hawkers of 60.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Eleven aspiring hawkers are currently operating incubation stalls, with another six awaiting allocation of incubation stalls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some of our new hawkers include Ms Priscilla Huang, aged 31, of Authentic Hong Kong Delights, and Mr Lim Wei Keat, aged 27, of Ah Keat Chicken Rice, who joined the hawker trade over the past year after completing HDP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition to Wei Keat’s chicken rice which we had for lunch just now, I have ordered mochi and water chestnut cakes from Priscilla for Parliament’s tea break today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A few others like Ms Amber Pong, aged 32, of The Headless Baker at Ghim Moh Market, who converted to a full-fledged hawker after completing her Incubation Stall Programme, even opened a second outlet in July last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To ensure that veteran hawkers’ recipes and skills are not lost, the Hawkers Succession Scheme (HSS), which was shared last year, will link retiring hawkers without succession plans but wish to pass on their businesses, skills and recipes, with aspiring hawkers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To Ms Pereira and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas’s question about the HSS, a 10-member independent advisory panel has been set up to work with NEA to support and review the HSS pilot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Among the 10 panellists, six are established hawkers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The rest include culinary chefs, hawker centre operators and culinary training partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The panellists will help identify suitable veteran hawkers, assess aspiring successors’ readiness, and provide feedback to improve the programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Under the pilot, aspiring hawkers will be assessed on culinary skills and capacity to learn, before pairing up with veteran hawkers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They will undergo a three-month apprenticeship under the veteran hawkers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Aspiring successors will be evaluated on their ability to execute the veterans’ signature dishes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Where needed, veteran hawkers may continue to mentor the successor for two additional months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is but a token of appreciation and is not a measure of the effort that veterans have invested into establishing their clientele and refining their recipes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The HSS is not intended to be a commercial arrangement but is an option to help retiring veteran hawkers find suitable successors and preserve their culinary legacy for future patrons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also introduce safeguards to protect the interest of the veteran hawkers such as requiring successors to serve the veteran hawkers’ signature dishes and retain the stall names for three years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Gan and Mr Wee asked about the construction progress of new hawker centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition, five more centres in the construction stage will progressively be completed in the next few years, and two more are in the planning and design stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Residents in Tampines Town can also look forward to another new hawker centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: More details of this new centre will be shared in due course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Nadia will be glad to hear that upcoming centres will incorporate sustainability features.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Two redeveloped centres will also be starting operations this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also expect Margaret Drive Hawker Centre, which replaces the hawker centre at Block 1A, 2A, 3A Commonwealth Drive, to commence operations from fourth quarter of 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: (In Mandarin):   NEA will be expanding the smoking prohibition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The smoking prohibition will also cover recreation sites under ABC Waters projects, as well as 10 recreational beaches, including three at Sentosa.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In the past two years, the Government has been supporting our hawkers through various ways and schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This includes waiving a total of 10 months of rent and subsidising six months of table-cleaning and centralised dishwashing fees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Eligible hawkers received up to $9,000 of income relief in 2020 and $500 in cash assistance last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To continue our support for hawkers, we will provide all SFA-licensed market, hawker centre, coffeeshop, food court and canteen operators and stallholders with a one-time cash assistance, under the recently announced Small Business Recovery Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Those who do not hire local employees will also receive a $1,000 payout.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Over the past four years, we have also been attracting new hawkers to join the trade through various training programmes and over 40 new hawkers have joined the trade through these programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will continue to support aspiring hawkers to enter the trade, including matching them with retiring hawkers via the Hawkers' Succession Scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They are at Bukit Panjang, Sembawang, Sengkang and Punggol respectively, and will provide residents in these towns with food choices and convenience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also be building a new hawker centre in Tampines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Lastly, from 1 Apr, Market Street Hawker Centre will return to its original site, and reopen on the 2nd and 3rd floors of the newly developed, large integrated development CapitaSpring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: All the original stallholders from "Golden Shoe" centre will return to the reopened Market Street Hawker Centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: (In English): Chairman, despite the challenges of the pandemic, everyone – be it the cleaning industry, premises managers or hawkers – have demonstrated resilience, seized opportunities to improve cleanliness, and embrace new business opportunities online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Let us continue to work together to build a truly SG Clean Singapore and safeguard our hawker culture for future generations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Chairman, I will be speaking about how MSE has taken steps and will continue to secure our food sources and water supply and how we intend to do this with the support of our industry as well as with every Singaporean.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Minister Grace Fu mentioned earlier that climate change and pandemics, such as COVID-19, are some of the biggest threats we face today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Coupled with the war in Ukraine, the confluence of factors is causing global supply and price volatility and we can expect to feel the impact in the coming months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our "grow local" basket is supported by our 30-by-30 goal – an ambition to expand our capability to grow more food locally in a sustainable and resource-efficient manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Last year, I shared about how our intention to masterplan Lim Chu Kang and turn it into a high-tech agri-food zone that can significantly raise food production and thereby also providing new and exciting job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I am glad to update Mr Don Wee and Prof Koh Lian Pin that in 2021, we completed a six-month-long series of engagements on how the Government, industry, including our farmers, nature groups and public can co-create the future Lim Chu Kang region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many industry players and other stakeholders are keen to embrace high-tech farming, with also other ideas like shared processing and distribution facilities and centralised waste management systems for complementary uses which will enhance the entire farming ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The feedback and ideas that we received from the engagements will now be folded into our actual planning phase of Lim Chu Kang this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We have also been driving research innovation and plugging existing technological gaps.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I echo Dr Lim Wee Kiak’s point that alternative proteins, such as cell-based and plant-based meats, can contribute to our nutritional needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As some alternative proteins do not have a history of use as food, it is important to ensure the safe introduction of such novel food products into Singapore's market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is why SFA developed the Novel Food Regulatory Framework in 2019 which requires companies to undertake pre-market food safety assessments as part of the process of seeking approval from SFA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I encourage novel food companies to engage SFA early through platforms, such as SFA's Novel Food Virtual Clinics, to better understand SFA’s requirements, so that they can prioritise their research efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Now, let me move on to our aquaculture industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Chairman, fish is a commonly consumed source of protein that can be grown locally to contribute to our food security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To Ms Nadia Samdin’s question, SFA has been working closely with the industry over the past year to understand their needs and introduce best practices that can help them uplift their production and the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I have joined them in some of these engagements and visited many of the farms in the Johor Straits as well as in the Southern Waters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The sea-based fish farms in Singapore are, indeed, quite varied, each with a unique approach to farming.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Some, like Rong-Yao Fisheries, culture their fish in traditional open-net cage systems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With good farm management practices in place, Rong-Yao Fisheries has obtained the Good Aquaculture Practice (GAP) Fish Farming certification.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We have also seen the emergence of high-tech farms which have the potential to transform fish farming by culturing fish intensively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Eco-Ark by Aquaculture Centre of Excellence (ACE) is one of the world’s first purpose-built floating closed containment aquaculture production structure that combines Offshore & Marine Technology with a closed containment system, using water treatment technology to provide good quality seawater to culture the fish and, at the same time, reduce the vulnerability to external conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Farms like Rong-Yao and ACE's Eco-Ark have found farming methods that work for them, but they also shared their hopes of getting greater certainty on their use of sea space so that they can continue to invest in their future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The charges will be progressively stepped up to market rate from 2023 to 2026.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Presently, most carbon offset programmes often serve as little more than a palliative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Typically, parties interested in reducing their carbon footprint, the climate-conscious non-profit hoping to attend an environmental conference on the other side of the world, say, will purchase offsets from a vendor or exchange equivalent to the amount of carbon that they expect to generate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, such vendors are seldom closely regulated and depend on the goodwill and enterprise of the operators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Too often, even among well-meaning vendors, the strategy is to simply pay off some rancher, who would otherwise cut down trees on their land, using the cash from the non-profit with a small fee paid to the vendor for the effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The system works well, of course, for just about everyone involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The ranchers benefit from a stream of income for not developing their land, the non-profit believes that they have done their part in reducing their carbon footprint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And the vendor has earned a transaction fee, all while believing that they are doing good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The typical scenario sketched out above is such that net emissions will actually have increased.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is where a credible system of offsets, paired with an actual cap-and-trade exchange, comes in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The major difference between this approach and that of a green vendor is that there it is no longer a counterfactual of otherwise increased carbon emissions that are being funded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, it is now used to fund activities that have to be backed up by actual verifiable emissions reductions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is where trusted governments can take a lead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A private-public partnership (PPP) led by private sector initiative and efficiencies, but encompassing active public sector involvement to ensure that the programme's purported goals are being met, strikes me as the best way forward for such an endeavour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I still hold to that position, which is shared by the majority of economists who have studied the merits of both systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, I see little reason why, if we are going to operate a carbon emissions trading system alongside a carbon tax regime, the system should not also be operated in a manner that complements our carbon reduction efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, a PPP of this nature is consistent with the stated goals of the Singapore Green Plan to develop Singapore as a carbon services and trading hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Credible carbon offsets can be a major project to help develop Singapore's trusted reputation in the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, all markets require liquidity and the best way to get the programme off to a solid start is to provide a steady stream of income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These will operate in line with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even better, if the Government takes on the proactive role of permanently retiring offsets that it purchases, then I think the world, the Earth in particular, will be much better off.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, during last year's debate, I spoke about the importance of Singapore building a world-class carbon trading ecosystem so that we can use high-quality carbon offsets to help us exceed our NDC.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also recently spoke about the importance of promoting carbon accounting/auditing services, as well as the importance of influencing the direction of global regulations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, I commend Singapore's new net-zero ambitions and our efforts to shape Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also hope that we can, if we use globally traded carbon credits, source for credits from many, rather than a few countries, because sourcing diversity also builds resilience for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Also, I hope carbon credits will supplement, rather than replace our local efforts to improve energy efficiency, import and generate green energy, and adopt mitigation technology, such as Carbon Capture and Sequestration.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, in sum, can MSE share more about our thoughts on how to best balance Singapore-based efforts versus the purchase of overseas carbon credits?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Chairman, Singapore needs to set up an appropriate carbon price mechanism to internalise the emissions cost and incentivise reductions effectively while ensuring we do not impose unbearable burdens upon our enterprises and households.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry elaborate on how the revised carbon tax levels and trajectory will support our objective of becoming a green economy?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We are faced with overall rising costs due to the pressures of the pandemic and other crises.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In the midst of this, we have begun to transit to use more clean and alternate energy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I understand that the Government sets a high threshold to limit compliance costs by smaller emitters.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But smaller emitters, those emitting at least two kilo-tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, are already “reportable facilities” and have to pay the costs of monitoring and measuring their emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Given that any additional compliance costs would likely be minimal, it makes sense for the carbon tax to cover all reportable facilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This would, after all, be in the spirit of a whole-of-nation fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Emitters, small and large, have a role to play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will the Government expand coverage of the carbon tax to include all reportable facilities?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Mr Chairman, the Singapore Green Plan 2030 was greatly welcomed when it was launched last year.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With the national agenda on sustainability set out, it creates a clear framework to rally a whole-of-nation movement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can the Government provide an update on our progress thus far for the Green Plan and what are the additional programmes and goals?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Considering the impact of the pandemic, are we still on track to reach the targets of the five pillars of the Green Plan – City in Nature, Energy Reset, Sustainable Living, Green Economy and Resilient Future?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: For example, are labour shortages delaying the development of new parks, greener buildings and the goal of producing locally 30% of our national nutritional needs by 2030?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How successful have we been in getting green investments and green jobs?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Have Singaporeans managed to conserve more water and electricity in the past year?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Research and development hold the key to our green aspirations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How would the Government direct its R&D funding to achieve Singapore Green Plan outcomes?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Are we attracting and nurturing enough talents in green and sustainability engineering, R&D and related technological explorations?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What impact has our R&D investments into sustainability and climate resilience projects made?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will we encourage more Singaporeans to take up deeper research in this field as a career?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: In 2020, about 52% of the 5.88 million tonnes of solid waste generated were recycled.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The rest were incinerated and sent to our only landfill – Semakau Island Landfill.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: We must expedite measures to reduce waste in the next few years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will the Ministry consider more drastic measures, such as higher fees or fines, to reduce waste generation?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the Ministry’s plans after this date?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will it extend the lifespan of Semakau Landfill?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Are there any updates on the progress of this initiative?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, to build a low carbon future, we do need to invest in R&D projects to address our special needs and requirements.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How will the Government direct its R&D funding to achieve the Singapore Green Plan outcomes?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Which are the areas with the best growth and development potential and how will the Ministry support them?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, the Singapore Green Plan 2030 was launched in 2020 with a slew of ambitious targets across the five pillars.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In light of Singapore’s increased ambitions, as announced in Budget 2022, and also inputs from the Members from the two Motions on Sustainability this and last year, whether the Government is making any adjustments to our Green Plan targets to match this increased ambition.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: The Government has made commendable efforts in engaging the public on the Singapore Green Plan 2030 and Budget 2022 and has continually encouraged public participation through public consultations.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Will the participating Ministries in the upcoming Green Plan conversations consider putting in place guidelines and protocols for greater accountability and transparency in the engagement process, including releasing post-engagement reports of key insights to the public?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Furthermore, it is laudable that the Ministries have conducted online public consultations on issues, such as the future of Dover Forest and the proposal for retailers to charge for plastic bags.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: However, the length of time allocated for seeking public feedback often varies between consultations for different issues, ranging from several weeks to months.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Has the Ministry canvassed feedback from the participants of these consultations and the public to better assess the most appropriate length of time for conducting public consultations?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Will the Ministry consider ways of ensuring sufficient time be allocated for future public consultations for the public to be more fully aware of issues and to provide even more valuable comments?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: One of RIE2025's key focus areas is urban solutions and sustainability, which will address challenges in sustainability and climate resilience.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: How does the Government intend to direct its funding under the USS domain to achieve Singapore Green Plan 2030 outcomes and to scale up innovation and enterprise to unlock green growth opportunities?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Does the Government have any early examples of the returns on our R&D investments into sustainability and climate resilience for Singapore?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: How much of this fund has been dispersed so far and, of which, how much has been resourced from our carbon tax revenue?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Additionally, does the Ministry have any early examples to share regarding the impact of the E2F since its inception?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: How can communities and individuals continue to participate in the national movement to secure a greener future for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: The SG Eco Fund was launched in November 2020 and aims to support projects that advance environmental sustainability and involve the community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: What is the progress of the SG Eco Fund so far?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: The Woodgrove community is one of the beneficiaries of this wonderful initiative.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Its community partner, the Singapore Institute of Building Limited (SIBL) has successfully applied for the SG Eco Fund, intending to raise awareness on environmental issues and encourage more residents to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle through community, education programmes, sustainable markets along with an app with interactive games.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Workshops will also be conducted with the support of our Woodgrove's green taskforce involving residents and volunteers to share useful tips to practise the 5Rs – refuse, reduce, repair, reuse and recycle – and to empower residents with the knowledge to conserve water and energy as well as to reduce food waste.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Looking at the list of the SG Eco Fund awardees, many of them have interesting and practical ideas.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Moving forward, I would like to ask if MSE would consider remodeling the SG Eco Fund concept so that more constituencies and divisions can consider applying for the grant to adopt ideas that have proven successful in other divisions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Apart from the finances, there is also a need to look into improving the existing infrastructures in our community so that individuals and the community are able to practise green living, such as building more community gardens and setting up more recycling bins catering to different recycling purposes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Many of my Woodgrove residents have shared that the present design of the blue recycling bin poses many challenges to recycle effectively.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Are there plans to roll out new types of recycling bins to replace the existing blue bins?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Rather than providing one bulk container for people to dispose all types of their recyclables and waste, can the Ministry consider and introduce more innovative solutions to encourage single-type recyclables?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: As we approach nine months since the results of the first grant call, I would like to ask what is the progress of the SG Eco Fund so far?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Given the wide-ranging sizes and types of projects which it has supported, what environmental and community outcomes does the SG Eco Fund track to ensure that the projects are achieving their goals and do these contribute towards our national targets and Green Plan?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Further, how can the SG Eco Fund better reach out to the community and are there ways for the Eco Fund to collaborate with the private sector for catalytic and sustainable funding as well as capacity building?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Residents can expect transformations which will enhance their built environments so that they will be more green, sustainable and liveable for residents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: For example, hawker centres will aim for zero waste by composting food scraps.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: In addition, these towns will be able to track their energy consumption, water usage, carbon emissions and their progress in recycling.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on what has been implemented so far and what future developments can be expected?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Will new waste disposal methods, such as a pneumatic waste conveyance system (PWCS), be introduced in these towns?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: How about the installation of more energy-efficient light bulbs and solar panels?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Will there be incentives for more rooftops to be converted to urban farming?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Will the Ministry facilitate community collaborations for recycling projects and electricity and water conservation drives?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, heat inequality is an issue I spoke on in last year's climate Motion in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The cheapest air conditioners cost about 60 cents per hour for electricity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, many less well-off residents head to air conditioned spaces like malls and libraries, which are important for the hottest days in the year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is not always space at the library though.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we quickly provide good stopgap measures for such vulnerable areas?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We already know where the warmest areas in Singapore are through Landsat thermal images and these places often have high concentrations of HDB rental blocks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We could focus our OneMillionTrees project on areas where vulnerable people live.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We also have a programme providing vouchers for households to buy high-efficiency appliances like fridges but can we extend this to include fans and include more households?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Blue collar workers face the short end of the stick.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For shift workers, it can be really hot sleeping during the day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This reduces sleep quality and quantity, which have an impact on workplace safety.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Studies show that driving on low-quality sleep can be as dangerous as drink-driving.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With migrant workers, many have spoken about why they choose to sleep on the floor or on hard boards without bedding.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The heat can be unbearable because, very often, you have 16 workers in a room and many dormitories have metal roofing and walls.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: NEA recently released a Good Environmental Health Practices statement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, there are no legally binding measures regarding heat management.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With the MOM employers' guide for domestic workers, there is no definition for "adequate ventilation".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2017, one of our non-governmental organisations (NGOs) even reported that a domestic worker was made to sleep on the balcony.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Of course, most employers put in effort to ensure workers have decent living conditions but let us work towards stricter binding guidelines so that no worker is left behind.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, executing on our Singapore Green Plan (SGP) 2030 is an imperative, whether it is all of us using less plastic bags or NUS researchers finding ways to store CO2 below ocean floor.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Like the COVID-19 pandemic, no country is spared, no business can ignore, no individual can hide.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We need the collective will of all of humanity to heal the earth for which we are all stewards of.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In this Committee of Supply, I would like to touch on the following points.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The SGP 2030 vision is a great rallying cry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How successful has our engagement of businesses and the public been and what are the next steps being taken?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The national Chambers are reiterating the importance for local companies to step up and embrace sustainability practices and standards urgently to better support their multinational companies (MNCs) partners based in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The race to create competitive green supply chains to stay relevant in the global economy and win is fast and furious.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How are we planning to create competitive green supply chains out of Singapore?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Besides that, Singapore is also blessed with: (a) having the world's busiest container transshipment port with a global network of more than 50 locations in 26 countries around the world; and (b) our Changi Airport, albeit pre-COVID-19, being the most internationally connected airport in Asia Pacific and among the top 10 air mega hubs in the world, according to OAG.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How can Singapore businesses leverage these two crown jewels to play the bigger game in this world of green and sustainable?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Ministry ensure a robust financing ecosystem will be in place to support the industry, especially the SMEs?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: More assistance schemes may be needed to catalyse the SMEs with specific actions.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Switching their fleet of vehicles to electric vehicles (EVs) will be a good first step but SMEs must not be mistaken that they can get to net zero without changing their processes and greening their supply chains.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, if players in the supply chain collaborate through research to innovate and partner each other and the Government to achieve progressive outcomes, the Government can provide more tax incentives.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The sustainability agenda will require leadership and talent with new skills and expertise and the collective will to act.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If you would like to take your both cuts together, please do.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Budget 2022 has outlined Singapore's ambitious plan to achieve net zero emissions by 2050 or around 2050.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To achieve this goal, there will need to be an accelerated pace of transition.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The green economy announced last year as Singapore's Green Plan 2030 sets out Singapore's objective of sustainability as a new engine of opportunity and growth for Singapore and investments to be carbon efficient.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is the Government doing to enable R&D to grow the capabilities of our industries to develop low-carbon alternative such as hydrogen and to advance other low-carbon sustainable technology and solutions?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, becoming more sustainable is not just about compliance for businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While companies will need to be able to address compliance, which often relates to regulations on emission, waste management, energy efficiency and labour practices, compliance also concerns investors' and consumers' decisions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, businesses need to understand the benefits, competitive advantage and growth opportunities of being a sustainable business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the unpredictability and instability in energy cost and supply, there is also direct business benefits of reduced cost for businesses to be more energy efficient and in having more sustainable operations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we know that to become greener and more sustainable does not just happen.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Companies will have to understand and track the impact of their business on the environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses need to also review and relook at how they produce their goods and deliver services, their supply chains to reduce waste and impact on the environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will require new skills and know-how as well as new systems and tools to manage.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What are the Government's key efforts to support businesses to transition and to capture value in the green transition?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is the Government doing to enable businesses to adopt more sustainable operations and develop sustainability as a competitive edge?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, in past speeches, I have called for Singapore to have a higher ambition, leading the way to a green future in spite of our size.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To do this, our local industry must innovate and invest in a green transition.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But uncertainty over costs, benefits and risks will influence incentives to make the move.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Each sector has a different emissions profile, transition readiness, industry structure and willingness of the end customer to pay.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The increase in carbon taxes may compel companies to move, though it must be implemented in just transition.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government is also exploring and putting in more regulations and standards and benchmarks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What else can the Government do to encourage local companies to invest, perhaps, ahead of the market?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And often account for a large share of their suppliers' revenues.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: However, public procurement is complex and highly decentralised and there are competing priorities and socioeconomic considerations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, does HDB prioritise going for the fastest, cheapest way to get a lot of flats out or go for green buildings that have lower embedded emissions and reduce controllable lifecycle emissions?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These are complex questions but ones which we must take a position and communicate effectively to all stakeholders as part of the green public procurement transformation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We can also invest in relatable and inspiring public education campaigns to educate Singaporeans on the choices they make.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For the right portfolio of measures and pace of implementation, we will need to understand trade-offs, consider cross-sector impact and socioeconomic impact.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will the Government support local companies that innovate and invest in a green transition ahead of the market?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to activate the market demand and willingness to pay, including among end consumers?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I filed the cut but I do not have to write my own speech here as the hon member Koh Lian Pin has very succinctly made the points in his Budget speech.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In a green economy, every worker must have basic and foundational knowledge of climate sustainability alongside functional specific skills and sector‐specific competencies to enable a successful transition of key industries towards sustainable business models and practices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our IHLs can play a key role in building these capabilities and competencies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to reskill and upskill employers, employees and students for managing and capturing value in the green economy?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad, would you like to report progress?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, should I take two cuts together?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Chairman, the Singapore Green Plan 2030 is well-timed to galvanise a national movement, not only to achieve sustainable development but also to build exportable capabilities, such as sustainable urban solutions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Our green agenda holds much promise for our future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Singapore is well-positioned to serve as a living lab and test bed for emerging green technologies as well as a hub to foster collaboration and co-creation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: With successive carbon tax increases in the pipeline, as well as increasing demands from partners, investors and customers for sustainable practices, SMEs need support to pivot and adapt, in order to thrive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: First, we can promote sector-based sustainability roadmaps with industry-aligned principles, frameworks and uniform standards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Second, we need to support SMEs with pre-identified sector-based green solutions to fast track their adoption.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Third, we can leverage the ecosystem to build scalable green capabilities and collaboration.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, nature-based climate solutions are powerful methods of carbon capture.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They also have the added benefit of protecting ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As we move to set up our carbon trading hub and companies consider buying carbon credits from overseas entities to offset emission, there is a pressing need to ensure projects are socially sustainable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lack of local buy-in, poor oversight and poor management can result in projects with less carbon capture than what companies pay for.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Indonesia's Katingan Mentaya project has reportedly been one such case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Poor quality credits diminish accountability and reduce the emissions captured.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Renewable projects funded by Government-linked companies (GLCs) should also be accountable for Environmental, Social, Governance (ESG) impacts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Reports mentioned that the Laos hydro projects could be negatively impacting food production, ecosystems and indigenous communities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With Keppel recently signing its hydroelectricity import deal, I hope that our GLCs pay attention to such externalities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Impacts can be minimised with the adoption of free prior and informed consent policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is important from the standpoint not only of promoting green outcomes, but for our national brand as well, Lastly, my Parliamentary colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, previously expanded on the potential soft power benefits of having a foreign aid agency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such an aid agency could support targeted cash transfers to indigenous and rural communities to manage and protect forests abroad.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: NGOs, like Cool Earth, already do this and one UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) report studying Latin America found this to be a cost-effective way to preserve forests.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, as Singapore positions itself to become a leading climate services hub, we need to develop a healthy pipeline of talents for our green economy.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Are there plans to consult the public, private and people sectors, including IHLs, businesses, green groups and our youth, on the demand, content and modes of delivery for these training and upskilling programmes?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: To build a vibrant and impactful sustainability ecosystem in Singapore, we should welcome and, indeed, encourage the participation of international organisations, including research and educational institutes, service providers and non-profits, to contribute to Singapore's efforts in building a green talent pipeline towards our sustainability goals.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But, crucially, to ensure success for Singapore's sustainability goals, we need to work closely with international stakeholders to build a common and deep understanding of Singapore's existing capabilities and gaps, ongoing efforts and investments and long-term vision and mission for sustainability, so that they might truly engage, collaborate and uplift our local enterprises, IHLs, civil society groups and other Singapore stakeholders.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: What steps is the Government taking to ensure that all stakeholder participation in our sustainability journey will be well-coordinated, complementary and synergistic to ensure that all stakeholders work towards the common goal of building a Singapore core of talents and expertise to achieve our sustainability ambitions?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, Minister Tan See Leng mentioned that Singapore could harness its robust legislative commodity trading and financial services foundation to develop an international trusted carbon services and training ecosystem here.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Other countries, like China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, are all taking steps to establish its own carbon markets or frameworks to trade carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to coordinate a holistic inter-agency effort to create a vibrant marketplace with many active participants with clear ESG and carbon credit standards in place.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At present, carbon markets are plagued by low liquidity, scarce financing, inadequate risk management services and limited data availability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We will need to further encourage our financial institutions (FIs) to get involved to meet the liquidity and financing difficulties.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Market infrastructure should develop along with deliberate and calibrated regulation by MAS and MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, what would be the risk-weighted asset, or RWA, to be associated with carbon credits?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For FIs holding carbon credits, will we need clearing houses to mitigate risks?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the moment, the weights are high and unclear.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: MTI and MFA must engage our partners to ensure that our carbon credits will be accepted in other countries, too.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We may need to provide it in our Free Trade Agreements so that other countries cannot take protection and discriminatory approach.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Further, given our lack of natural resources, including land, we are unlikely to have any huge wind farms or hydroelectric plants that can originate a large amount of carbon credits for sale.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We, therefore, require our agencies like EDB to go out and attract project developers to bring and sell their carbon credits in Singapore with an "ASEAN Registry" of sorts set up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We will also need to train the necessary subject matter expertise in our workforce, whether through our tertiary institutions or our various work training programmes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will we expect to see a detailed roadmap outlining how and when we will get there?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the most far-reaching crises today is the global energy crunch.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Increased fuel consumption from an economy recovering from COVID-19, production outages and geopolitical events have driven up prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Presently, almost 95% of Singapore's electricity is generated using imported natural gas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, our push to transition into a low-carbon energy future cannot come at a more opportune time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, given our limited size, what challenges does the Government expect with energy transition and what measures have been put in place to ensure a smooth transition?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For Singapore, solar energy appears more promising than other renewable energy sources like wind or hydro.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will we look to incentivise individual households to install their own solar panels to defray their own consumption?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as the founding director of Green SG, a registered charity that aims to catalyse and accelerate green action and develop future leaders for sustainability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is looking for alternatives from Algeria and Azerbaijan.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In Germany, there were thoughts of cancelling plans to shut down nuclear plants and ramp up coal-powered generators.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Heavy industries are affected and are reducing production and shortening of working hours.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Power generation infrastructure cannot be built over a short period of time.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are well reminded of the 1973 oil crisis caused by the OPEC embargo; the 1990 oil shock caused by the Gulf war; 2001 California electricity crisis caused by market manipulation by Enron.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And to remember that peak oil is on the horizon and oil production will go on a terminal decline.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must, therefore, plan our energy transition well, well-diversified with price stability and affordability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How we plan our energy transition will affect future generations and the security of our economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, I would like to ask the Minister to share more on expected challenges ahead and how the Government will ensure a smooth energy transition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: What is our latest progress and future plans for our solar deployment?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How will our energy transition impact future electricity prices?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Pre-pandemic, transport accounted for 16.2% of Singapore's carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is already a lower percentage than the US, UK and the global figure, but it is still a significant piece as we look out to cut our carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What are the Ministry's plans to reduce transport emissions on land, air and sea?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: A key pillar of our efforts to decarbonise our transport system is the adoption of electric vehicles, or EVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: To successfully do so, we must make EVs a financially sensible option for users, capitalise on rapid technological advancements and ensure that our infrastructure is integrated to support this switch to EVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Presently, a major obstacle to private adoption of EVs is the prohibitive costs involved.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Vehicle prices in Singapore are already among the world’s highest, with our COE system to control the vehicle population in land-scarce Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This discourages the uptake of EVs and is likely preventing a wider choice of EVs from entering the Singapore market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We may need to relook how our EVs are classified for COE purposes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Another question is whether the existing incentives and rebates for EVs are sufficient to affect consumer behaviour to the desired level.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Given Singapore's car-lite strategy, we probably cannot afford to give EV owners a two-year road tax exemption like how Malaysia has done.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, we do need to study our incentive and rebate structure to see if any revisions are necessary.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For example, I understand that road tax for EVs is currently based on the simple addition of the power output of its motors and this may lead to weird situations where an EV is taxed based on a total added output of 390 kW even though it can only deliver a maximum combined output of 240 kW.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Harnessing technological advancements can also promote the adoption of EVs by enhancing convenience and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Battery swapping technology has been tried and tested in markets like China and Norway and represents a more efficient proposition to users than electric charging at charging stations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This could complement our existing strategy of building more EV charging points closer to where people live.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We must reassure the people that EVs are a safe option before they can decide to embrace it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Ministry share more about its overarching strategy to further stimulate EV adoption among road users in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Would the Minister consider introducing an early adoption incentive for electric motorcycles?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Most of the individuals who bought EVs are likely to stay in landed properties due to the high cost of EVs and the ease of installing mid-range EV home chargers for about $2,500 at the comfort of their home.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Can MOT shed some light on the demographics of the first wave of EV buyers in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare my interest as I work in the transport industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I have always maintained that whether EVs can take off in the mass market segment is dependent on whether we have sufficient public charging stations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If we leave it to market forces, few will be willing to install charging stations in large numbers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, it is very important for Singapore to decisively incentivise companies to build EV charging facilities ahead of demand, like what the European countries and China have been doing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In particular, I would like to suggest four areas for MOT to consider.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, I would urge the Government to consider paying for the upgrading cost of the grid and the expansion of the electric substations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Second, to encourage the growth of the EV mass market segment, the Government can consider providing significant incentives for companies to install up to five charging stations at all HDB car parks that have a sizeable number of parking lots.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Third, for condominiums, few MCSTs are successful in installing the charging stations because they need to go through a long and tedious process to obtain the residents’ support.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Could LTA work with MND to consider mandating all condominiums with a sizeable number of parking lots to install charging stations?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would it be possible for the Government to provide incentives for doing so, especially for the early adopters?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Fourth, would the Government consider mandating all commercial properties, including shopping centres and malls with sizeable parking lots, to install charging stations?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: After solving the supply side of installing charging stations, we need to provide incentives to increase the ownership of EVs, like what Norway and China have been doing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In Norway, almost 65% of all new passenger cars sold in 2021 were EVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Norway government taxed internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles very heavily, but does not tax EVs at all.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The reduction in the excise duty should be inversely proportional to the EV’s OMV, so that there would be a bigger discount for a cheaper EV.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This would prevent profiteering by EV distributors and make EVs more affordable to the masses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can expect emission improvements from passenger cars as we require all newly-registered vehicles to be cleaner-energy models from 2030.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the Ministry’s plans to reduce transport emissions?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government increase the use of incentives for the use of EVs and other clean energy vehicles?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the steady increase in EV adoption and EV charging, will the Government set up a dedicated certification centre to oversee the safety and reliability of EVs and their charging points and batteries?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the progress to set up a framework for the industry's safety standards for EVs and EV batteries permitted in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry give an update on EV adoption so far and whether the set-up of charging points and provisions for battery changes are on track?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry encourage more private participation, including the utilities companies, as what other countries have done, to set up and offer EV fast-charging services as well as battery changing services?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Transiting to a greener transportation sector will require quicker adoption of EVs by users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry consider further incentives and tax rebates to encourage the purchase and use of EVs, including commercial vehicles, such as vans, buses and coaches?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Ministry facilitate and expedite the electrification of our public transport fleets?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In embracing EVs, perhaps the biggest hurdle in the smooth transition to popular adoption of EVs is the issue of infrastructural coordination.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, what is the schedule like for charger deployment and how would this be synced with the gradual adoption of EV models?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will there be priority given to livelihood vehicles like taxis and PHVs at charging docks?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would the Government regulate the cost of charging?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could the Ministry give a clearer account of the overall plan on how the charger deployment will be financed and accelerated?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This, however, only represents 0.5% of the 645,000 cars in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, this uptick is encouraging, considering that much of it was contributed by the increase of 924 units in the number of Tesla's here in Singapore, which costs about S$200,000 each.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The economics of EVs currently is still such that it is difficult for the average Singaporean to adopt EVs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe more can be done to ensure that we phase out ICE vehicles ahead of 2040, especially in the context of Singapore's COE system.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Norway, for example, saw 84% of new car sales in January being all electric.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as EV prices start to come down with advancements in manufacturing, the disparity in price between EVs, after factoring in Government incentives, are still significant.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This reduces the attractiveness of EVs to consumers at a time where we should be pushing forward for adoption.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Government will also consider longer-term policies, such as preferential access and toll rates, which have been shown to show a significant impact on boosting EV sales in Oslo and several Chinese cities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We also need to accelerate the rollout of EV-charging points across Singapore to further incentivise EV adoption and ensure it is both economical and practical for Singaporeans to adopt EVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The increase in our green ambitions requires us to look at emerging trends in last-mile logistics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This has meant great convenience to Singaporeans who purchase from online platforms, but it also is likely to mean that there is more demand for last mile logistics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Today, all types of goods vehicles are of the diesel engine variety.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The increase in demand for last-mile logistics will mean an increase in our carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The accelerating effects of COVID-19 would have increased the carbon emissions more rapidly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To be clear, the Government has taken some steps to mitigate the issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: During the COS last year, then Minister for Transport Ong Ye Kung made the announcement that no new diesel cars and taxis will be allowed to be registered from 2025.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The current Commercial Vehicle Emissions scheme, which started in April last year, was designed, in part, to persuade owners of light commercial vehicles, which make up 68.9% of all goods vehicles, over to vehicles that burn cleaner fuels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We have also seen electric light commercial vehicle models increasingly being rolled out by manufacturers, such as Renault, Opel and BYD.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The main constraint is electric charging infrastructure, which is still in its infancy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I, therefore, wish to seek updates from the Minister on the plans for a green transition for such goods vehicles, starting with an update on the Government's targets to convert goods vehicles to EVs and other green options and plans to achieve these targets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the Ministry be getting more industrial estate operators to roll out more EV charging infrastructure around industrial areas and encourage a switch to electric light commercial vehicles and vans?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will there be subsidies for companies that adopt these EVs early?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Chairman, the EV charging sector is growing rapidly with the acceleration of EV adoption.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Has the Ministry considered the need to strengthen regulations on EV chargers and EV charging operators, to ensure a safe and reliable charging network?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: The Government has announced targets for the greening of our public transport and point-to-point fleets by the year 2040.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Will the Ministry be announcing further details of our EV roadmap, particularly in relation to any intermediate targets for the greening of our public transportation fleets, similar to what has been done for private vehicles?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Chairman, at MND's COS 2021, I said that for urban infrastructures to be more climate-resilient, it is imperative to adopt the use of existing climate change information and resources for urban planning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Further, to have buildings designed with lower carbon emissions and for sustainable maintenance, we should incorporate innovative design solutions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The Government announced then that it is driving R&D in urban sustainability, such as climate-resilient urban infrastructure with reduced carbon emissions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on the progress made and how the Government plans to encourage stakeholders to adopt these solutions further?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Often, when people think of sustainable projects, they will, naturally, associate it with higher costs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, that is because they did not consider sustainable principles in the project planning for building lifecycle costs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By optimising resources during the planning stage to evaluating environmental and performance trade-offs, finding a good balance between capital and lifecycle costs, it can effectively improve the outcome of the system.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The push towards a low-carbon built environment also has to do with scale, speed of adoption and investment in technologies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When larger players in the value chain utilise good asset management programmes and invest in technologies at scale, the trickle-down effect will benefit the smaller players, too.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With emerging trends in sustainability towards dynamic master planning for city planning or utilities, I believe we can leverage algorithms and digital tools to predict and test extensive scenarios to better organise capital allocation, project prioritisation and develop strategies to improve the city’s resilience and liveability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With all these giving momentum to the industry and deepening research for solutions, we will soon be able to put sustainability concepts into real-world practice.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I would thus like to ask BCA: apart from the sustainability guidelines, as introduced for existing and new buildings, how is BCA supporting the industry to effectively transit to a low-carbon built environment?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To do so, we can look at R&D and talent development.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The Government announced last year it is driving R&D in urban sustainability.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Can MND update on the progress of the efforts in R&D?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As the R&D topics are so wide-ranging, does it make sense to focus on specific areas, such as coastal protection and issues unique to the region or the tropical belt?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This can help us focus, as well as differentiate, our capabilities.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Can the R&D be commercialised by Singapore companies and developed into exportable services?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The built environment (BE) sector will be the key sector that needs to be transformed to fulfil our future urban sustainability needs.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: However, the built sector has difficulty attracting more talent.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To build up a critical mass of talents, we should have a holistic approach.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For example, curriculum in schools and tertiary institutions should be updated and jobs redefined to better reflect the new capabilities needed.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It may also be useful to reframe the built environment jobs to better reflect their contribution.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Jobs in this sector are not just about building things.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, they help to enhance our liveability, support our economy with intelligent infrastructure while allowing us to be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We should also seek more ways for public-private sector collaboration.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The aims are two-fold: one, to help employees with continuous learning and upgrading of their professional skills; two, to help employers better recognise and reward higher skill levels.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Can MND comment on how to better build up a critical mass of talents in urban sustainability?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially reflected in its plans for urban development.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We can do so by designing and constructing greener buildings.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: How will BCA continue to support our transition to a low-carbon built environment?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is also driving R&D in urban sustainability.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is to ensure that our urban infrastructure is made more climate-resilient while reducing carbon emissions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: May we please have an update on the progress made so far?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: How will the Building and Construction Authority support our transition to a low-carbon society?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: The Government announced during the Committee of Supply 2021 that it was driving R&D in urban sustainability with the goal of enhancing the climate resilience of our urban infrastructure while reducing their carbon footprint.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: May we please have an update on the progress made so far?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
